Hi Dad,

Here is what happened in AI today. Each item links to the full story, with plain-language explanations of anything unfamiliar. The links go to a website built especially for you, with a new edition every day, so do check it out.

Question of the day: Does YouTube really lock you inside a bubble of videos you already agree with? You watch one video about making cheese at home, and the next day your whole feed is cheese. Many people fear the same thing happens with opinions. The answer is at the end of this email.

  • Google: for the first time, attackers have been caught letting AI find and exploit security holes with no human involved. Google’s security researchers say that for the first time they have found attackers who handed the whole job of breaking into websites to AI. The system watches for repairs to popular website software, works out from each repair where the weakness was, writes a break-in program and runs it against sites that have not yet updated, all without a person. The targets appear to have been French websites. For now such attacks are fast but clumsy and easy to notice. The advice is the old one: install updates promptly. Read more and the background.
  • A physicist says OpenAI’s model helped him prove a step towards a fifty-year-old goal in particle physics. An American physicist, Nathaniel Craig, says OpenAI’s AI model helped him take a step towards a goal physicists have pursued for about fifty years: writing the full theory of elementary particles in a form a computer can calculate with. The idea was his; the model, he says, did much of the detailed proof, and three specialists then read it. The author himself calls it “much more a beginning than an end”. The paper has not yet been reviewed by a journal, and the author is currently working at OpenAI. Read more and the background.
  • The United States extends an AI adviser for air traffic to the whole country, sooner than planned; humans keep the final say. The United States has extended an AI adviser for air traffic to the whole country. The system, called SMART, gathers weather, flight plans and other data and suggests how to route flights around jams; specialists check each suggestion, and controllers have the final say. The authorities say that in two months around Washington it rerouted 180 flights and saved 10 minutes each on average. The controllers’ union says it was not consulted, and members of Congress have asked for an audit of how the system was tested. Read more and the background.
  • AI now tops the list of worries about the US financial system in the central bank’s survey. In the US central bank’s twice-yearly survey of financial professionals, AI has come top of the list of worries about the financial system. The fears: AI companies’ shares are very expensive and could fall sharply; AI makes attacks on banks easier; and the building of data centers is being paid for with fast-growing debt, more than $680 billion borrowed this year against $130 billion in the whole of 2023. The report does not predict a crash, and only 23 people were surveyed. Read more and the background.

Also on the website today: Anthropic on how an AI should keep notes for itself: the skill is knowing what to leave out, Alibaba releases a new flagship model that competes mainly on price, Apple starts a study of how people use AI for health questions.

Answer to the question of the day. Partly, but the effect on what people believe seems much smaller than is often feared, according to the Russian magazine Sistemny Blok. More than 500 hours of video are uploaded to YouTube every minute, so a program has to choose what to show you. It looks at what you have watched and searched for, what you subscribe to, what you liked and how long you kept watching, and also at what people with similar tastes enjoyed. The result is a “filter bubble”: you see mostly what matches your earlier choices. People add to it themselves, since we all tend to look for confirmation of what we already think. Does this change minds? Here the article is careful. In one large study, researchers built an imitation of YouTube in which they could control the recommendations, and ran four experiments with nearly 9,000 people. Those kept in a “bubble”, where three of every four suggestions matched their views, did watch a narrower range of videos, but their political opinions, their trust in the media and their attitude to opponents barely moved. A test of the “rabbit hole” idea, that ever more extreme videos make the viewer more extreme, found no notable effect either. The author’s conclusion: there is no convincing proof so far that recommendation programs change beliefs, though they do narrow what we see, and long-term effects remain an open question. Her advice is simple: compare sources and now and then go looking for another point of view on purpose. Sistemny Blok, “Filter bubbles on YouTube: benefit or risk?” (September 2026) (article in Russian).
